## Remarks

The first diagram displays the open deformation family $D_i=M\setminus B$,
with structure map $p$ induced by $M\to\mathbb P^1$. Both squares are
Cartesian: $j$ includes the special fibre, while $u$ includes the complement
of that fibre. Here $\mathbb A^1=\mathbb P^1\setminus\{\infty\}$; the local
parameter $t$ used above vanishes at $\infty$, not at the origin of this
ordinary-fibre chart.

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large, font=\Large, labels={font=\large}]
C_XY \arrow[r, hook, "j"] \arrow[d] & D_i \arrow[d, "p"] & Y\times\mathbb A^1 \arrow[l, hook', "u"'] \arrow[d] \\
\{\infty\} \arrow[r, hook] & \mathbb P^1 & \mathbb A^1 \arrow[l, hook']
\end{tikzcd}
```

For the full blowup family, write $E=\mathbb P(C_XY\oplus1)$ and
$W=\mathbb P(C_XY)$. Its infinity fibre is the divisor $B+E$, with each
summand occurring once. The second diagram shows the closed inclusions into
that fibre and their common boundary $W=B\cap E$. Removing $B$ leaves
$E\setminus W=C_XY$, the special fibre of $D_i$.

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large, font=\Large]
W \arrow[r, hook] \arrow[d, hook] & E \arrow[d, hook] \\
B \arrow[r, hook] & M_\infty
\end{tikzcd}
```

The projective completion $E$ is a projectivized cone in general; no regular
immersion is assumed in either diagram. Only under the regular-immersion
hypothesis stated above is $C_XY=N_{X/Y}$ a vector bundle. At the level of
cycles, flat pullback along $Y\times\mathbb A^1\to Y$ raises dimension from
$m$ to $m+1$; localization lifts this class to $A_{m+1}(D_i)$ and $j^!$
lowers dimension to $m$, yielding the stated $\sigma_i$. The chart and
localization arguments above establish these facts independently of the
figures.

## Remarks

The right-hand square displays the middle matching in the source-first order.
Here $v'(x_i,x_j,x_k)=(x_i,x_j)$, $u'(x_i,x_j,x_k)=(x_j,x_k)$,
$u(x_i,x_j)=x_j$, $v(x_j,x_k)=x_j$, and $h(x_i,x_j,x_k)=(x_i,x_k)$.
Thus $uv'=vu'$ and $T_{ijk}=Z_{ij}\times_{X_j}Z_{jk}$; the arrow $h$ is
proper by the base-change description in the definition.

```tikzcd
[font=\LARGE, every label/.append style={font=\Large}, column sep=large, row sep=large]
Z_{ik} & T_{ijk} \arrow[l, "h"'] \arrow[r, "v'"] \arrow[d, "u'"'] & Z_{ij} \arrow[d, "u"] \\
& Z_{jk} \arrow[r, "v"'] & X_j
```

The same matching gives the following order of operations on Borel–Moore classes:

```tikzcd
[font=\LARGE, every label/.append style={font=\Large}, column sep=large, row sep=large]
H_{p+q}^{\mathrm{BM},G}(Z_{ij}\times Z_{jk})
\arrow[r, "\Delta_{X_j}^{!}"] &
H_{p+q-2d_j}^{\mathrm{BM},G}(T_{ijk})
\arrow[r, "h_*"] &
H_{p+q-2d_j}^{\mathrm{BM},G}(Z_{ik})
```

The input is $a\boxtimes b$, with ordered coordinates $(i,j,j,k)$.
The first arrow matches the middle pair using the positively complex-oriented
normal bundle $TX_j$ and lowers degree by $2d_j$; the second forgets the middle
point. The sheaf exchange for the right-hand square is precisely
$v'^*u^!\to u'^!v^*$, with no assertion that it is an isomorphism on arbitrary
supports. These diagrams only illustrate the definition; its well-formedness
and the cited compatibility proofs remain independent of the figures.

## Remarks

The ring maps underlying base change and localization fit into the following commutative squares. Write $f\colon A\to B$ for the given map and $g\colon A\to A'$ for the base-change map.

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large, every cell/.append style={font=\Large}, labels={font=\large}]
A \arrow[r,"f"] \arrow[d,"g"'] & B \arrow[d,"i"] & A \arrow[r,"f"] \arrow[d,"\ell_A"'] & B \arrow[d,"\ell_B"] \\
A' \arrow[r,"j"'] & B' & V^{-1}A \arrow[r,"\bar f"'] & U^{-1}B
\end{tikzcd}
```

Here $i(b)=b\otimes1$ and $j(a')=1\otimes a'$. The left square is the tensor-product pushout of [F2]: $i(f(a))=j(g(a))$. On the right, $\ell_A(a)=a/1$, $\ell_B(b)=b/1$, and $\bar f(a/v)=f(a)/f(v)$; the hypothesis $f(V)\subseteq U$ makes $\bar f$ well defined. This square commutes because both paths take $a$ to $f(a)/1$.

For $B'=B\otimes_AA'$, the differential comparison is the commutative triangle of $B'$-modules below. The tensor product in its upper-left corner is over $B$, whereas the two differential modules on the right have different base rings.

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large, every cell/.append style={font=\Large}, labels={font=\large}]
B'\otimes_B\Omega_{B/A} \arrow[r,"\alpha"] \arrow[dr,"\varphi"',"\cong"] & \Omega_{B'/A} \arrow[d,"q"] \\
& \Omega_{B'/A'}
\end{tikzcd}
```

The map $\alpha$ is the functorial comparison of (3) for $i$, and $q$ sends $\mathrm{d}_{B'/A}x$ to $\mathrm{d}_{B'/A'}x$. Thus $q\alpha=\varphi$: on $1\otimes\mathrm{d}b$, both paths give $\mathrm{d}_{B'/A'}(b\otimes1)$, as in step 2.1. Only $\varphi$ is marked as an isomorphism here. Its inverse is induced by the $A'$-derivation $D(b\otimes a')=a'(1\otimes\mathrm{d}b)$ from step 1.1. For localization, step 1.2 instead uses $D(b/u)=u^{-1}\mathrm{d}b-bu^{-2}\mathrm{d}u$ and identifies $U^{-1}\Omega_{B/A}$ with $\Omega_{U^{-1}B/V^{-1}A}$; [F3] identifies its source with $(U^{-1}B)\otimes_B\Omega_{B/A}$.

These diagrams illustrate the maps already constructed in the proof; the proof is independent of the figures.

## Remarks

For the chase in step 4.1, fix $n$ and abbreviate $J=\mathfrak m^n$, $A=(I\cap J)\otimes_R M$, $B=(I\otimes_R M)\oplus(J\otimes_R M)$ and $C=(I+J)\otimes_R M$. For an ideal $L$, write $\mu_L:L\otimes_R M\to M$ for multiplication. The following diagram displays the right-exact tensor row and its compatibility with multiplication:

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large]
A \arrow[r,"\alpha"] \arrow[d,"\mu_{I\cap J}"'] & B \arrow[r,"\beta"] \arrow[d,"\mu_I\oplus\mu_J"] & C \arrow[r] \arrow[d,"\mu_{I+J}"] & 0 \\
M \arrow[r,"\delta"'] & M\oplus M \arrow[r,"\sigma"'] & M \arrow[r] & 0
\end{tikzcd}
```

Here $\alpha(x)=(i(x),-j(x))$, where $i:A\to I\otimes_R M$ and $j:A\to J\otimes_R M$ are induced by the ideal inclusions; $\beta$ is induced by addition into $I+J$. The lower maps are $\delta(m)=(m,-m)$ and $\sigma(u,v)=u+v$. Both squares commute: multiplication agrees with each ideal inclusion, and multiplication after addition equals the sum of the two multiplication maps. The top row is exact by [F20]; no injectivity of $\alpha$ is asserted.

For $k\in K$ as in step 4.1, $\mu_{I+J}\beta(k,0)=\mu_I(k)=0$. The injectivity of $\mu_{I+J}$ from step 3.1 gives $\beta(k,0)=0$, so exactness lifts $(k,0)$ to some $x\in A$. Thus $i(x)=k$ and $j(x)=0$, and $\mu_{I\cap J}(x)=\mu_Jj(x)=0$. The diagram illustrates this lift and its sign convention; the rigorous proof above is independent of the figure.

## Remarks

Put $W=U\cap V$ and suppress the common coefficient ring $R$. With the orientations on $U$, $V$ and $W$ restricted from $M$, the commuting ladder is

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=large, /tikz/font=\Large, labels={font=\large}]
H_c^p(W) \arrow[r, "{(e_U,-e_V)}"] \arrow[d, "D_W"'] & H_c^p(U)\oplus H_c^p(V) \arrow[r, "e_U+e_V"] \arrow[d, "D_U\oplus D_V"] & H_c^p(M) \arrow[r, "\delta"] \arrow[d, "D_M"] & H_c^{p+1}(W) \arrow[d, "D_W"] \\
H_{n-p}(W) \arrow[r, "{(i_{U*},-i_{V*})}"'] & H_{n-p}(U)\oplus H_{n-p}(V) \arrow[r, "i_{U*}+i_{V*}"'] & H_{n-p}(M) \arrow[r, "{(-1)^{p+1}\partial}"'] & H_{n-p-1}(W)
\end{tikzcd}
```

Here the first horizontal maps use the inclusions of $W$ into $U$ and $V$, and the second use the inclusions of $U$ and $V$ into $M$. Both rows are segments of exact sequences. The rightmost vertical map uses cohomological degree $p+1$, so its target is $H_{n-p-1}(W)$. The first two squares express open naturality from step 1.1. For the last square, the connector convention is $[z_U+z_V]\mapsto[\partial z_U]$; steps 6.1–7.1 give $\partial D_M=(-1)^{p+1}D_W\delta$, hence $(-1)^{p+1}\partial D_M=D_W\delta$. No vertical arrow is asserted to be an isomorphism. The proof above establishes these relations independently of the diagram.

## Remarks

The fiber-product square defining the exchange mate is Cartesian:

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large, scale=1.5, transform shape]
T=A\times_M B \arrow[r,"a"] \arrow[d,"b"'] & A \arrow[d,"q"] \\
B \arrow[r,"u"'] & M
\end{tikzcd}
```

The graph factorization in step 3.1 fits into the following two Cartesian squares. Here $\Gamma_q(x)=(x,q(x))$, $\theta(x,y)=(x,y)$, and $\Delta(m)=(m,m)$.

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large, scale=1.5, transform shape]
T \arrow[r,"a"] \arrow[d,hook,"\theta"'] & A \arrow[r,"q"] \arrow[d,hook,"\Gamma_q"] & M \arrow[d,hook,"\Delta"] \\
A\times B \arrow[r,"\mathrm{id}_A\times u"'] & A\times M \arrow[r,"{(q,\mathrm{id}_M)}"'] & M\times M
\end{tikzcd}
```

The bottom composite is $F=(q,u)$, while the top composite is $qa=ub$. Thus the outer rectangle identifies $T$ with $F^{-1}(\Delta(M))$, as used in step 2.1. Pulling the supported morphism $g_\Delta$ first through the right square and then through the left gives $g_F$ by the proper-base-change identifications in steps 2.1 and 3.1. The factorization of $q$ itself is $q=\operatorname{pr}_2\circ\Gamma_q$. These diagrams record the supports and maps only; the orientation, adjunction and counit arguments remain those of the proof, independently of the illustrations.

steps.before: 4.1 Base change and finite flat normalization. Consider a cartesian square with $f:X\to Y$ proper and $g:Y'\to Y$ flat of pure relative dimension $n$, and write $f':X'=X\times_Y Y'\to Y'$ and $g':X'\to X$. For an integral $d$-dimensional $V\subseteq X$, put $W=\overline{f(V)}$ and $e=\dim V-\dim W$. If $e>0$, both $g^*f_*[V]$ and $f'_*g'^*[V]$ are zero: every component of the flat pullback of $V$ has dimension $d+n$, while its image has dimension at most $\dim W+n<d+n$. If $e=0$, set $m=[k(V):k(W)]$. For each component $W_i$ of $g^{-1}(W)$, let $C_i$ be the Artinian local ring of $W\times_Y Y'$ at its generic point. Flat pullback gives coefficient $\ell(C_i)$ on $[W_i]$. The generic algebra of $V\times_Y Y'$ over $C_i$ is $C_i\otimes_{k(W)}k(V)$, a free $C_i$-module of rank $m$. Decomposing it into its Artinian local factors shows that the sum of the generic lengths of the components above $W_i$, weighted by their function-field degrees over $k(W_i)$, is $m\ell(C_i)$. These are precisely the coefficients of $[W_i]$ in $f'_*g'^*[V]$ and $g^*f_*[V]$, respectively. Hence the base-change identity holds on cycles and therefore on Chow groups. Finally, if $f$ is finite flat of constant degree $n$ between integral schemes of the same dimension, then $f$ is dominant and $[k(X):k(Y)]=n$, so $f_*[X]=n[Y]$ by step 1.1. [F1, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

remarks.after:
## Remarks

The base-change assertion in step 4.1 involves two squares. The first is
Cartesian, with $X'=X\times_Y Y'$ and the two projections $g'$ and $f'$:

```tikzcd
[column sep=large, row sep=large, font=\Large]
X'=X\times_Y Y' \arrow[r, "\textstyle g'"] \arrow[d, "\textstyle f'"']
& X \arrow[d, "\textstyle f"] \\
Y' \arrow[r, "\textstyle g"'] & Y
```

Here $f\circ g'=g\circ f'$. The vertical maps are proper, and the horizontal
maps are flat of pure relative dimension $n$. Pushforward follows the vertical
arrows, whereas flat pullback reverses the horizontal arrows. Thus the second
square has the following directions and dimension indices:

```tikzcd
[column sep=huge, row sep=large, font=\Large]
Z_d(X) \arrow[r, "\textstyle g'^*"] \arrow[d, "\textstyle f_*"']
& Z_{d+n}(X') \arrow[d, "\textstyle f'_*"] \\
Z_d(Y) \arrow[r, "\textstyle g^*"'] & Z_{d+n}(Y')
```

Its commutativity is $f'_*g'^*=g^*f_*$, proved in step 4.1; the same square
holds with $A$ in place of $Z$. The degree is dimension, so proper pushforward
preserves the index and flat pullback increases it by $n$. This does not
assert that proper pushforward preserves codimension. For an integral
$V\subseteq X$, the equal-dimensional case retains the full coefficient
$m=[k(V):k(W)]$, where $W=\overline{f(V)}$: the generic-length computation in
step 4.1 gives $m\ell(C_i)$ at each component $W_i$ above $W$. No assumption
that these field degrees or generic lengths equal one is made, including
over a nonclosed field. In the dimension-drop case both routes give zero.
The diagrams illustrate the maps and their grading; the proof above remains
independent of them.

steps.before: 8.1 Sections of smooth morphisms. Let $s:T\to P$ be a section of a smooth morphism $P\to T$ of constant relative dimension $r$, with $T$ locally Noetherian. Near a point $t\in T$, [F8] factors $P\to T$ Zariski locally as an étale morphism $P'\to\mathbb A^r_T=\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O_T[x_1,\dots,x_r]$ followed by the projection, after shrinking around $s(t)$ and $t$; by [F7] the étale morphism is flat. The composite $T\to P'\to\mathbb A^r_T$ is the graph of the $T$-point with coordinates $c_i=s^*(x_i)$. This graph is cut out by the regular sequence $x_1-c_1,\dots,x_r-c_r$: after quotienting by the first $i$ terms, the next element is a monic linear polynomial in a new variable and hence a nonzerodivisor over any base ring. Pulling the graph back along the flat étale map $P'\to\mathbb A^r_T$ gives a regular immersion $Q=T\times_{\mathbb A^r_T}P'\hookrightarrow P'$ of codimension $r$, and $Q\to T$ is étale. The section factors through a section $T\to Q$ of this étale morphism. By [F8], after shrinking near the chosen point, this section is described by a standard étale chart $\operatorname{Spec}((A[z]/(P))_g)\to\operatorname{Spec}A$ with $z\mapsto a$, $P(a)=0$ and $P'(a)$ a unit. Factoring $P(z)=(z-a)Q_0(z)$ gives $Q_0(a)=P'(a)$; after restricting to the open neighborhood where $Q_0$ is invertible, the equation $P(z)=0$ forces $z=a$, so the section is an open immersion there. Hence near its image in $P'$, the pulled-back regular equations cut out $s(T)$, proving that $s$ is a regular immersion of codimension $r$. These equations remain regular after every base change $T'\to T$, since the section of the smooth base change $P\times_TT'\to T'$ is again locally obtained by this graph construction, including when $T'$ is singular. The normal bundle also commutes with base change: for a section of a smooth morphism, the conormal bundle identifies with $s^*\Omega^1_{P/T}$, and this relative differential bundle pulls back to $s'^*\Omega^1_{(P\times_TT')/T'}$. Hence the codimension and normal bundle are preserved by arbitrary base change on $T$. [F7, F8, algebra] ∎

remarks.after:
## Remarks

The two exact sequences in step 4.1 are sequences of locally free
$\mathcal O_X$-modules. Write $\alpha([f])=1\otimes df$ and let $\beta$ be
restriction of differentials to $X$. Their ranks are respectively $d,m,n$, with $d=m-n$:

```tikz
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large, every cell/.append style={font=\large}]
0 \arrow[r] & \mathcal I/\mathcal I^2 \arrow[r, "\alpha"] & i^*\Omega^1_{Y/k} \arrow[r, "\beta"] & \Omega^1_{X/k} \arrow[r] & 0
\end{tikzcd}
```

Applying $\mathcal Hom_{\mathcal O_X}(-,\mathcal O_X)$ reverses the order;
$T_X=(\Omega^1_{X/k})^\vee$ and
$N_{X/Y}=(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2)^\vee$. There is no identification of a
bundle with its own dual in these pictures. The dual ranks are $n,m,d$:

```tikz
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large, every cell/.append style={font=\large}]
0 \arrow[r] & T_X \arrow[r, "\beta^\vee"] & i^*T_Y \arrow[r, "\alpha^\vee"] & N_{X/Y} \arrow[r] & 0
\end{tikzcd}
```

For the coordinate model of step 5.1, put $X_U=X\cap U$ and use coordinates
$(z_1,\ldots,z_d,v_1,\ldots,v_n)$ on $\mathbb A^m_k$.
The étale map $\varphi$ pulls $z_j$ back to $f_j$ and $v_a$ back to $u_a$.
The following square is Cartesian: its bottom inclusion is cut out by
$z_1=\cdots=z_d=0$.

```tikz
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large, every cell/.append style={font=\large}]
X_U \arrow[r, hook] \arrow[d, "\varphi|_{X_U}"'] & U \arrow[d, "\varphi", "\mathrm{etale}"'] \\
\mathbb A^n_k \arrow[r, hook] & \mathbb A^m_k
\end{tikzcd}
```

To see how this model controls the deformation blowup, restrict to the
chart $\mathbb A^1_t\subset\mathbb P^1_k$ on which $t=0$ is $\infty$.
Set $V=U\times_k\mathbb A^1_t$, $M=\mathbb A^m_k\times_k\mathbb A^1_t$,
$C=X_U\times_k\{0\}$ and $C_0=\mathbb A^n_k\times_k\{0\}$.
Thus $C_0\subset M$ has ideal $(z_1,\ldots,z_d,t)$, whose inverse image
under $\psi=\varphi\times\operatorname{id}$ is the ideal
$(f_1,\ldots,f_d,t)$ of $C$. Write $B_V=\operatorname{Bl}_C V$ and
$B_M=\operatorname{Bl}_{C_0}M$. Step 6.1 and flat base change give the
Cartesian square

```tikz
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large, every cell/.append style={font=\large}]
B_V \arrow[r] \arrow[d, "\pi_V"'] & B_M \arrow[d, "\pi_M"] \\
V \arrow[r, "\psi", "\mathrm{etale}\ (\mathrm{hence\ flat})"'] & M
\end{tikzcd}
```

The vertical arrows are the blowup morphisms; the top arrow is the base
change of $\psi$, so is étale. This identifies $B_V$ with
$V\times_M B_M$, rather than identifying the global blowup with the model.
The $d+1$ model charts are the $t$-chart with coordinates
$(z_1/t,\ldots,z_d/t,t,v_1,\ldots,v_n)$ and, for each $1\le j\le d$, the
$z_j$-chart with coordinates
$(z_j,(z_l/z_j)_{l\ne j},t/z_j,v_1,\ldots,v_n)$; each has $m+1$ coordinates.
All affine spaces and products in these pictures are over the given field
$k$; no assumption that $x$ is $k$-rational is made. The bundle ranks are
those over $\mathcal O_X$, or dimensions after tensoring with $\kappa(x)$,
not the local-ring dimensions $m-\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(x)$ and
$n-\operatorname{trdeg}_k\kappa(x)$ of step 1.1. These diagrams illustrate
steps 4.1, 5.1 and 6.1; the proof above remains independent of them.

steps.after: 1.2 Conversely, assume every filtered colimit functor is exact. Let $I$ be a small directed poset indexing an increasing family of monomorphisms $b_i:B_i\rightarrowtail A$, and let $c:C\rightarrowtail A$ represent a fixed subobject of $A$. For each $i\in I$, form $P_i=B_i\times_A C$ with projections $p_i:P_i\to B_i$ and $q_i:P_i\to C$, so $b_i p_i=cq_i$; the composite represents $B_i\wedge C$ by [L4]. For $i\le j$, the inclusion $u_{ij}:B_i\to B_j$ induces the unique $v_{ij}:P_i\to P_j$ with $p_jv_{ij}=u_{ij}p_i$ and $q_jv_{ij}=q_i$. Thus the pullback squares form a diagram indexed by $I$. Set $B=\operatorname*{colim}_I B_i$ and $P=\operatorname*{colim}_I P_i$, with induced maps $p:P\to B$, $q:P\to C$, and $b:B\to A$. The colimits of the constant diagrams at $A$ and $C$ are canonically $A$ and $C$, since $I$ is nonempty and directed. Exactness and [L2] therefore imply that the induced square, with relation $bp=cq$, is again a pullback, namely $P\cong B\times_A C$. The same preservation of finite limits makes $b$ monic, since the natural transformation $(b_i):(B_i)\to\operatorname{const}_I A$ is pointwise monic. Both squares are illustrated in Remarks. [L2, L3, L4, assume-hyp, construct]

The first square is the pullback defining $P_i$ in step 1.2; the second is its filtered-colimit square. The labels are the maps defined there, and both squares commute: $b_i p_i=cq_i$ and $bp=cq$. In the second square, $B=\operatorname*{colim}_I B_i$ and $P=\operatorname*{colim}_I P_i$, while $A$ and $C$ arise from constant diagrams. The pullback property of the second square uses the assumed exactness of $\operatorname*{colim}_I$.

## Remarks

The supplied orientation makes both nonzero rows constant-coefficient rows.
On page $n+1$, the following schematic shows two columns of these rows;
all intermediate rows are zero. Here $a\geq0$ and the diagonal arrow has
bidegree $(n+1,-n)$.

```tikzcd
[font=\Large, labels={font=\large}, row sep=3em, column sep=4em]
E_{n+1}^{a,n}=H^a(B;R)u \arrow[dr, "d_{n+1}" description] & E_{n+1}^{a+n+1,n}=H^{a+n+1}(B;R)u \\
E_{n+1}^{a,0}=H^a(B;R) & E_{n+1}^{a+n+1,0}=H^{a+n+1}(B;R)
```

For $x\in H^a(B;R)$ the diagonal sends $xu$ to
$(-1)^a x\smile e(p)$; at $a=0$ it sends $u$ to $e(p)$.
Taking its cokernels in the bottom row and kernels in the top row gives the
two stable terms of proof step 3.1. Their short exact filtration sequence
then gives (1): $p^*$ factors through the bottom-row cokernel, while $p_!$
is the top-row quotient followed by its inclusion, using the orientation,
into $H^{k-n}(B;R)$. The cup maps in (1) retain its stated sign normalization.
The schematic neither asserts a splitting of the filtration nor identifies
$p_!$ with a cohomological axis edge; the proof above is independent of it.

remarks.after:
## Remarks

For a fixed coefficient group $G$, the following exact-row fragment displays
all three types of naturality square, including the degree-lowering connector.
Here $i_*$ is induced by subspace inclusion, $q_*$ by the quotient of chain
complexes, $f_A=f|_A:A\to B$, and $f_{\mathrm{rel},*}$ is the relative homology
map induced by $[c]\mapsto[f_\#c]$.

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[font=\Large, labels={font=\large}, column sep=large, row sep=large]
H_n(A;G) \arrow[r, "i_*"] \arrow[d, "(f_A)_*"'] &
H_n(X;G) \arrow[r, "q_*"] \arrow[d, "f_*"] &
H_n(X,A;G) \arrow[r, "\delta_{X,A}"] \arrow[d, "f_{\mathrm{rel},*}"] &
H_{n-1}(A;G) \arrow[d, "(f_A)_*"] \\
H_n(B;G) \arrow[r, "i_*"'] &
H_n(Y;G) \arrow[r, "q_*"'] &
H_n(Y,B;G) \arrow[r, "\delta_{Y,B}"'] &
H_{n-1}(B;G)
\end{tikzcd}
```

The right square says $(f_A)_*\delta_{X,A}=\delta_{Y,B}f_{\mathrm{rel},*}$.
For a relative cycle represented by $c$, the connector is represented by
$\partial c$ in the subspace, and $f_\#\partial c=\partial f_\#c$ gives this
identity with no extra sign. These are relative chain quotients, not a claim
identifying relative homology with the homology of a quotient space. The proof
above is independent of the diagram.

remarks.after:
## Remarks

Write $P=\mathbb P(\mathcal E)$ and denote the isomorphism in the statement
by $\Phi_d$. Proper pushforward detects its last summand, as the following
commutative square illustrates:

```tikzcd
[column sep=huge, row sep=large, font=\Large]
\displaystyle\bigoplus_{i=0}^{r-1} A_{d+i}(X)
  \arrow[r, "\textstyle\Phi_d", "\textstyle\sim"']
  \arrow[d, "\textstyle\mathrm{pr}_{r-1}"']
& A_{d+r-1}(P) \arrow[d, "\textstyle\pi_*"] \\
A_{d+r-1}(X) \arrow[r, equal] & A_{d+r-1}(X)
```

Here $\operatorname{pr}_{r-1}(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{r-1})=\alpha_{r-1}$.
For each $i$, flat pullback first sends $A_{d+i}(X)$ to
$A_{d+i+r-1}(P)$, and capping with $\xi^i$ then lands in the common group
$A_{d+r-1}(P)$. Proper pushforward preserves this homological dimension;
its target in the square is therefore $A_{d+r-1}(X)$. Step 1.1 shows that
$\pi_*(\xi^i\cap\pi^*\alpha_i)$ vanishes for $i<r-1$ and equals
$\alpha_{r-1}$ for $i=r-1$, proving the square commutes. This single
pushforward extracts only the last coefficient. The successive cap and
pushforward operations in step 2.1 apply after the already detected
coefficients have vanished in the relation; the square asserts no simultaneous
extraction of all coefficients. For $r=1$, it reduces to
$\pi_*\pi^*=\operatorname{id}$ with $\xi^0$ the identity operation.
The diagram illustrates the grading and the pushforward identities; the
proof above remains independent of it.

[font=\LARGE, every label/.append style={font=\Large}, column sep=large, row sep=large]

complexes on $X_i$. This square illustrates the adjunction chain; the proof

terminal_source_heading.before_suffix:
$\square$ ## Source qualification

Stacks Project Lemma 33.12.3 (tag 038V), lines 23–38, gives the affine-chart characterization of geometric regularity and its finite purely inseparable field tests. Lemma 33.12.6 (tag 038X), lines 23–28, proves that geometric regularity at a point is equivalent to smoothness there for a locally finite-type scheme. The latter statement does not assume perfectness; perfectness enters this item through the regular-algebra scalar-extension theorem. Stacks Algebra Lemma 10.166.1 (tag 0381), lines 22–36, gives the finitely-generated-field versus finite-purely-inseparable test. The stronger arbitrary-field scalar-extension assertion used here is supplied by the fully proved library item [[thm-ag-geometric-regularity-perfect-base]] via [[lem-ag-geometric-regularity-field-tests]].

Milne, *Algebraic Geometry*, Chapter 10 supplement, §f, item 10.64 (printed p. 18 / PDF page 18), states that a regular variety over a perfect field is smooth and that a smooth variety is regular. Milne's “variety” conventions are narrower than the present claim about arbitrary finite-type schemes and do not include this proof's nonreduced dual-number boundary; that citation is corroboration for the classical case, not a substitute for the scheme-level chart argument above.

The latter statement does not assume perfectness; perfectness enters this item through the regular-algebra scalar-extension theorem. Stacks Algebra Lemma 10.166.1 (tag 0381), lines 22–36, gives the finitely-generated-field versus finite-purely-inseparable test. The stronger arbitrary-field scalar-extension assertion used here is supplied by the fully proved library item [[thm-ag-geometric-regularity-perfect-base]] via [[lem-ag-geometric-regularity-field-tests]].

Milne, *Algebraic Geometry*, Chapter 10 supplement, §f, item 10.64 (printed p. 18 / PDF page 18), states that a regular variety over a perfect field is smooth and that a smooth variety is regular. Milne's “variety” conventions are narrower than the present claim about arbitrary finite-type schemes and do not include this proof's nonreduced dual-number boundary; that citation is corroboration for the classical case, not a substitute for the scheme-level chart argument above.

remarks.after:
## Remarks

The pullback square used in step 1.1 is

```tikzcd
P \arrow[r, "q"] \arrow[d, "p"'] & C \arrow[d, "c"] \\
B \arrow[r, "b"'] & A
```

Its commutativity is $bp=cq$, and the monomorphism representing the meet is $m=bp=cq:P\to A$.
